prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots, the quantum spin Hall and Z2 topological-insulator entry is the candidate with the broadest and most robust support: seven of eight members rank it, every one of them between second and fourth, and four place it in their top three. It is a clean theory-plus-experiment story. Kane and Mele made the decisive conceptual step, the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant band insulators with protected helical edge states. Molenkamp's group then observed quantized edge conduction in HgTe wells, which is a concrete, reproducible experimental discovery and not only a concept. More than fifteen years of independent confirmation by transport, ARPES and STM across many materials make the interpretation stable. It is a distinct advance from the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions, and I read it as timely to somewhat overdue rather than premature. I now put it above my own opening first choice, circuit QED, because that choice is the one where my field closeness and my WACQT role make my judgement least impartial, and because B012 has the broader and more consistent support.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that pointed to HgTe is not covered by the credited names, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional topological insulator stream (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Hasan; Cava) is a separate credit line that a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize would leave outside. A reasonable committee member could argue that the discovery framing is therefore contested and that a prize resting on a three-name limit would misrepresent how the field arose. There is also an argument that the 2016 prize already took the topological label and that the practical payoff of the quantum spin Hall edge channels remains limited because real-material edge conductance is imperfect.

responses.point: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the top choice: a clear Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 Jarillo-Herrero experiments, reproduced widely and reshaping a field, with credit shared as theory plus experiment.
responses.response: I agree that the prediction-then-discovery structure is strong and that it should stay among the alternatives. I disagree on timing and on credit. The superconducting mechanism is unresolved, as you note, and the field is still moving fast, so the lasting interpretation is not yet fixed. The experimental credit is also concentrated in one group while Cao and the parallel moire work sit outside the credited names. Topological insulators have the same attribution gaps, but there the physics has been settled for over a decade, which is why I place maturity ahead of novelty here. I would revisit B047 in a few years.

responses.point: Active-matter hydrodynamics (Vicsek, Toner-Tu, Ramaswamy) deserves first place as a coherent branch of nonequilibrium statistical physics, with long-range order in two dimensions and giant number fluctuations that are experimentally tested.
responses.response: The conceptual originality is real and I take the Mermin-Wagner point seriously. My reservation is breadth of agreement and discovery character: you are the only member who ranks it, and its experimental verification of the key exponents is partial, as you concede. It is also largely theory and model driven, with the experimental side spread over granular, colloidal and bacterial systems. I do not feel qualified to judge the renormalisation-group arguments in depth, so I would want to hear a statistical-physics assessment of how decisive the experimental tests are before treating it as a serious rival to B012.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest invention-type advance: Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's 1e-18 accuracy, mature in several laboratories and heading toward a redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree that this is a clean two-person configuration with no serious competing claim to the core idea, and it is the strongest of the non-topological options, which is why I list it as an alternative. My hesitation is that the discovery is a metrology instrument advance whose full recognition may come with the redefinition of the second, and the comb prize of 2005 sits in its lineage. It is also true that I am no atomic-clock expert, so I defer to you and Lindroth on the systematics. If the committee prefers a measurement achievement over a conceptual discovery, B019 is where I would go.

responses.point: Dynamical mean-field theory is the framework that made strongly correlated electrons tractable and links to first-principles materials calculation, and it is mature after three decades, though your opening admits your view is shaped by your own methods work.
responses.response: I accept the methodological importance and the maturity argument. My difficulty is that DMFT is an approximation scheme and not a discovery in the sense of the prize statute, and the attribution is crowded: Metzner, Müller-Hartmann and Jarrell are outside the credited names, so a Georges-Kotliar-Vollhardt prize would leave out the origin of the infinite-dimension limit. Topological insulators share some attribution difficulty but have a concrete experimental observation behind the theory, which I weigh more heavily.

responses.point: Gamma-ray burst afterglow localisation settled the cosmological origin of bursts and is overdue, with a plausible three-person split between the X-ray localisation and the optical redshift follow-up.
responses.response: I cannot judge the astrophysics in detail, but the point that the stable interpretation is nearly three decades old is persuasive. My qualification is that only you rank it, and your own text concedes that the optical follow-up involved other groups whose roles cannot be adjudicated from the supplied names. I would want to understand whether a fair three-name allocation exists before moving it above B012.

uncertainties: Whether a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize is acceptable given that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological-insulator contributors fall outside the credited names.
Whether the committee views the 2016 topological-phases prize as making a topological-insulator prize redundant.
Whether a superconducting-circuit prize (B004) is advisable in 2026, so soon after the 2025 macroscopic quantum tunnelling prize, which I cannot judge impartially.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene will be stable enough in interpretation, given the unresolved superconducting mechanism, for B047 to overtake B012 within a few years.
statement.conflict_note: I ranked circuit QED (B004) first in my opening ballot. Circuit QED is my own research field (circuit and waveguide QED), I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology at Chalmers, and my Chalmers colleagues and frequent collaborators, Per Delsing, C. M. Wilson and Anton Frisk Kockum, work in the same area, with Chalmers having hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I therefore advise that I should not carry weight on B004 and should be recused from any decision on it, and I have not placed it in my preferred configuration or alternatives. No specific personal or institutional conflict is apparent from my profile for B012, B047 or B019.
